original_excerpt: Malundi or owner of the mal is a shepherd who tends his own flock. But if someone is hired to look after the flock on wages, he is called a pohal... The pohals, when hired, are given (1) free meals, (2) free clothing and wool for the family, (3) two or four sheep per hundred sheep and goats and (4) Rs. 2/- in cash per month as wages.
neutral_summary: Differentiates owner-shepherds (malundi) from hired wage-shepherds (pohal), detailing customary remuneration in kind (food, clothing, wool, sheep dividend) and cash.
term_notes: Pohal derived from Pashupal; mal refers to pastoral flock.
coder_notes: Primary evidence of contractual pastoral labour in high-altitude transhumance.

original_excerpt: No one keeps a buffalo as the climate is not conducive to the proper rearing of buffalo. Once a villager brought a buffalo, but he was not happy with the experience as the milk yield suddenly dropped from 9 srs. to 4 srs. and the buffalo had to be taken to low hills before winter.
neutral_summary: Severe climate and high altitude prevent buffalo rearing in Brahmaur, causing sharp drop in milk yield and forcing winter removal to the plains.
term_notes: Seer (sr) is traditional measure (~0.93 kg); low hills refers to Kangra/Punjab borderlands.
coder_notes: Crucial explanation for complete absence of buffaloes in village census despite presence in OCR text.

original_excerpt: It is interesting to note that all the three blacksmiths and 2 silversmiths are Sipis and Reharas respectively. It will also be worthwhile to mention that the above table indicates only the primary occupations of the villagers, and instances are not lacking when a man with agriculture as his primary occupation has sheep and goats rearing as his subsidiary occupation.
neutral_summary: Artisanal metalworking is strictly stratified along caste lines (Sipis for ironwork, Reharas for silverware), while agriculture and pastoralism operate as multi-tiered subsidiary livelihoods.
term_notes: Sipi and Rehara represent artisan castes within the traditional Gaderan hierarchy.
coder_notes: Demonstrates caste-based craft specialization and dual livelihoods.

original_excerpt: The Sipis are the traditional weavers and tailors of the Gaddis. They wash the wool, spin it into yarn and weave the pattu and gardu blankets, and stitch the chola and dora.
neutral_summary: Sipis perform hereditary textile processing, weaving woolen tweed (pattu) and blankets (gardu), and tailoring the distinctive Gaddi costume.
term_notes: Chola is woollen frock; dora is black woollen rope sash; pattu is coarse woolen tweed.
coder_notes: Demonstrates essential economic interdependence in sheep-wool processing and attire.

original_excerpt: At the Shiva Nawala, the priest is usually a Brahman, but the Sipi acts as the traditional musician and drummer (dholak player) and receives the neck portion of the sacrificed sheep and grain.
neutral_summary: Ritual ceremony honoring Lord Shiva where Brahmin performs liturgical rites while Sipi provides sacred drumming and receives customary meat and grain shares.
term_notes: Nawala is central thanksgiving sacrifice to Lord Shiva among all Gaddi strata.
coder_notes: Direct proof of ritual interdependence across high and low caste boundaries.
